title: Regional evacuation fast-path — operator scratchpad
content:
Purpose and scope:

Quick reference for operators executing a rapid regional evacuation (fast-path) when telemetry indicates severe region-level degradation and there is imminent customer impact. This is intentionally compact: steps to make a deterministic, low-risk traffic diversion, plus short checks to reduce common post-shift regressions (kvcache warmup, edge TTLs, origin capacity). Not a replacement for the full playbook — this is the ‘get traffic out now’ flow.

When to use fast-path:
- Region shows sustained 5xx rate > 5% for 3 minutes AND error budget spike correlates with region-specific egress/edge metrics (not global).
- Active mitigation attempts (route throttles, local autoscale, instance restarts) failed or are progressing slowly and SLO burn rate > 10x.
- Business-critical customer sessions are timing out and SLAs are at risk.

High-level goals (in order):
1) Stop customer-facing requests landing in the degrading region.
2) Preserve session continuity as much as possible (cookies/route affinity tolerated for 2–5s default).
3) Avoid long token replays / model re-warm costs by pre-warming fallback caches where feasible.
4) Maintain observable signals to revert quickly when region improves.

Operator checklist (fast-path):
1) Pre-checks (30s):
   - Confirm incident lead and declare “fast-path” on incident bridge (Slack #sre-incident + page).
   - Snapshot key telemetry (last 5m): 5xx rate, p95 latency, origin error logs, edge egress error rate, peering errors. Attach URLs to incident.
   - Identify affected region code (e.g., us-west2) and impacted edge POPs.

2) Execute immediate routing change (60s target):
   Option A — Weighted shift via control plane (preferred if responsive):
     - Increase away weight from region -> 0.0 over 1–2 min with linear cadence. Apply to traffic tier(s): low/normal/high (do high first if customer-impacting).
     - Example: set routing weight for region us-west2 to 0.0 for route /v1/generate and streaming.
   Option B — DNS emergency (if control plane is degraded):
     - Lower region DNS records TTL to 10s if not already low (expect propagation delay).
     - Update weighted DNS to divert traffic to nearest healthy region. Do not change global park domain unless necessary.
   Option C — Edge-level blackholing (last resort):
     - Return 503 from edge for affected region and rely on global fallback. Use only when origin routing impossible.

3) KV cache considerations (1–4 minutes):
   - Trigger preseed for critical model KV caches in target region(s) where we expect sustained traffic. Use preseed job: infra/kvcache/preseed --models gpt-base,gpt-medium --target-region eu-west1 --priority high.
   - If preseed not possible, expect increased token generation cost and higher latencies for first few requests. Communicate to product if degradation extends beyond 10 minutes.

4) Autoscaling and capacity knobs (2–5 minutes):
   - Ensure fallback region has burst capacity: check Dedicated pool available capacity and trigger emergency autoscale policy if necessary (dedicated-cli capacity increase --pool fallback --temp 20%).
   - If fallback region lacks capacity, use cross-account spillover policy to route to hosted tier as temporary relief.

5) Observability after shift (0–10 minutes):
   - Watch these charts closely: global 5xx, fallback region p50/p95 latency, fallback region token generation rate, latency by model, end-user error rate, kvcache miss rate.
   - Set temporary alert thresholds: p95 > 2x baseline OR 5xx > 1% will automatically notify the lead.

6) Communication (immediate):
   - Post on incident channel: short summary (region, action taken, expected user-visible effect, TO-DOs). Use template: "Fast-path initiated for <region>. Diverted traffic to <region(s)>. Expected UX: short latency spike, no 5xx after shift. Investigating root cause."
   - Notify Customer Success for premium customers with open sessions in affected region.

Safety valves and rollbacks (if things get worse):
- If fallback region errors escalate (5xx rate > 2% sustained), revert weights by 50% toward original region while enabling circuit-breaker on heavy routes.
- If kvcache miss storm causes cascading origin overload, temporarily enable cached-only responses for low-priority routes (config flag: features.cached-only-low).
- If DNS TTL changes cause oscillation, revert TTL to previous and rely on control-plane weighted routing for smoother transitions.

Post-shift diagnostics (do these while monitoring):
- Correlate origin logs to identify root cause: instance OOM, network egress errors, peering flaps, colo power events.
- Check control-plane health: router agents, route decision logs, config push success.
- Verify that partial traffic to degraded region is not accumulating large KV cache entries that can cause eviction storms when re-enabled.

Short operator commands and queries (examples to paste into bridge):
- Snapshot recent 10m errors: monitoring.query "region:us-west2 AND status>=500 AND timeframe=10m"
- Set routing weight (control plane CLI): routing set-weight --route /v1/generate --region us-west2 --weight 0.0 --policy linear --duration 120s
- Lower DNS TTL (dns-admin): dns update-ttl --zone redwood-global --record region-us-west2.redwood.ai --ttl 10
- Trigger kvcache preseed: infra/kvcache/preseed --models gpt-3b,gpt-7b --target-region eu-west1 --parallel 4

Known gotchas / pitfalls (notes to self):
- Rapid TTL drops on some CDNs will be ignored due to upstream caching; expect ~60–90s practical propagation in some geographies.
- DNS shifts can re-route third-party clients differently because of resolver locality; prefer control-plane routing for API clients.
- Preseeding too many model variants can overload network egress; stagger by model size.
- Session affinity can cause percents of traffic to remain pinned to degrading region for 1–5 minutes — communicate this as expected.

Ownership and who to call (L1/L2):
- L1 SRE: run the fast-path checklist and set routing changes.
- L2 Serving-runtime: validate KV cache health and preseed jobs.
- L3 Networking: confirm peering and BGP anomalies are not blocking egress.
- Product/CS: craft customer-facing note if outage > 15m.

After-action todo (first 24h):
- Collect timelines and attach to incident. Who changed what (routing, DNS, autoscale)?
- Reproduce the routing scenario in staging with lower TTL DNS and kvcache warmup to calibrate timing.
- Add a decision-record for whether to automate the fast-path for future similar signatures.
- Run a capacity-increase playbook to ensure fallback pools can handle +30% sustained traffic for 1 hour.

Experiment hypotheses to test (backlog):
- Automate kvcache preseed trigger on detection of cross-region weight > 25% within 5 minutes.
- Simulate CDN resolver caching to measure real-world DNS propagation and update our TTL recommendations.
- Create an emergency cached-only mode for non-critical inference endpoints to limit origin churn.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- Can control-plane routing be made atomic across all tenant tiers (free/paid/dedicated) for faster coherent shifts? (Jira SRE-9123)
- Is a single global metric (region-health-score) feasible that reliably triggers fast-path without operator confirmation? (risk: false positives)

Quick paste templates (incident channel):
- Short status: "Fast-path active for <region>. Traffic diverted to <fallback>. Expect minor latency increase. Investigating root cause."
- Customer note (CS): "We detected degraded behavior in <region> and temporarily routed your requests to a healthy region; sessions should continue. We are monitoring and will update you in 15 minutes."

Notes to self (handy reminders):
- Prefer control-plane weight shifts over DNS when possible.
- Keep TTL changes as a backup and document resolver-level delays.
- Run kvcache preseed conservatively; prioritize small/medium models first.

Recent experiment logs (links):
- kvcache-preseed-loadtest-2025-01-12 (results: 2–4s p95 extra latency during preseed window; no origin overload)
- dns-ttl-propagation-sim-2024-11-05 (notes: some resolvers ignore TTL < 30s)

Finish: this file is a living scratchpad — append concrete command snippets and verified dashboard links as they are proven during drills. If you change any step for a live incident, add a one-line rationale to the incident timeline so we can iterate the playbook quickly.
